title: Responding to Writing Feedback
keyIdea: Good writers re-read their work out loud to check that it makes sense. When a reader asks a question, such as 'What did it look like?' or 'Why?', add a detail that answers that question, or a reason with 'because'. A star says what is good. A wish is a job to do, not a telling off. After each change, read the sentence again.

kid: Read your writing out loud. Does it sound right? If not, a word may be missing.
A reader may ask you a question. What did it look like? Where were you? Add words that answer that question. Big and spotty tell what a dog looks like. By the river tells where.
If the reader asks why, add a reason. Use the joining word because.
A star says what is good. A wish is a job to do. It does not mean your work is bad. After you change it, read it again.
adult: This is the start of revising, and children need an adult to guide it. The English National Curriculum asks Year 1 pupils to re-read what they have written to check that it makes sense and to discuss what they have written with the teacher or other pupils. In Year 2 they make simple additions, revisions and corrections. The US Common Core standard W.1.5 says the same in its own words: respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing.

Two skills sit at the heart of it. First, re-reading aloud: children often 'read' what they meant rather than what they wrote, so a missing word goes unnoticed until they point at each word as they say it. Second, matching a detail to the question. A common mistake is to add any detail at all. Asked 'What did the dog look like?', a child adds 'at the park', which is a good detail but answers 'where?'.

Use the proper words with your child: sentence, re-read, detail, describing word (adjective), joining word (conjunction) and 'because'. A noun with describing words in front, such as 'a big, spotty dog', is what Year 2 calls an expanded noun phrase. Two stars and a wish is a common classroom format, and many children at first hear a wish as criticism. Say plainly that a wish is a job, and that every writer gets them.

In the lab your child drops a missing word into the right gap and hears what a wrong gap sounds like, answers a reader's questions with details that fit, adds a reason with 'because', sorts stars from wishes, and taps each new detail in a before-and-after story.

familyTip: After your child writes or tells you a sentence, ask one question about it: 'What colour was it?' or 'Why?' Let them add the answer, then read the new sentence together, pointing at each word.

visual.caption: The question was 'What did the dog look like?' Does the detail answer it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: read back and add the missing word, answer a reader's questions with details, add a because reason, sort stars and wishes, spot new details.

practice.prompt: Sam wrote: 'I like to my scooter.' Read it out. What is wrong?
choices: It needs a full stop in the middle
practice.hint: Point at each word as you read it. Does it sound right?
practice.explain: A word is missing. 'I like to ride my scooter.' Reading it out loud helps you hear the gap.

practice.prompt: Mia wrote: 'I saw {n} birds.' Her teacher asks: 'Where were they?' Which change answers the question?
choices: I saw {n} birds in a tree.
practice.hint: The question is 'where?'. Find the words that tell a place.
practice.explain: 'In a tree' tells where. 'On Monday' tells when and 'little' tells what they looked like.

practice.prompt: Ben wrote: 'I was sad.' His friend asks: 'Why?' Which is the best change?
choices: I was sad because my toy broke.
I was sad because I was sad.
practice.hint: A reason tells what made it happen. Use 'because'.
practice.explain: 'Because my toy broke' gives a reason. 'Because I was sad' just says the same thing again.

practice.prompt: Your story has {n} sentences. Your teacher gives you two stars and a wish. What is the wish?
choices: A job to make your writing better
A sign your writing is bad
practice.hint: Stars say what is good. What does a wish ask you to do?
practice.explain: A wish is a job to do. It helps all {n} sentences get better. It is not a telling off.

pool.prompt: What is the best way to check your writing makes sense?
choices: Read it out loud, pointing at each word
pool.hint: How can you hear a missing word?
pool.explain: Read it out loud and point at each word. Then you read what you wrote, not what you meant.

pool.prompt: Tom wrote: 'I have {n} cats.' The question is: 'What do your cats look like?' Which detail fits?
choices: I have had {n} cats since Monday.
pool.explain: 'Fat' and 'ginger' are describing words (adjectives). They tell what the {n} cats look like.

pool.prompt: Which joining word adds a reason?
pool.explain: 'Because' joins a reason to a sentence: 'I wore a hat because it was sunny.'

pool.prompt: Your friend says: 'I like your word splash.' Is that a star or a wish?
pool.hint: Does it say what is good, or ask for a change?
pool.explain: A star. It tells you what is good, so keep doing it.

pool.prompt: Lily wrote: 'We played {n} games.' Her teacher asks: 'Who did you play with?' Which change fits?
choices: We played {n} games in the hall.
pool.hint: The question is 'who?'. Find a person.
pool.explain: 'With Nan' tells who. 'In the hall' tells where, and 'fun' tells what the games were like.

pool.prompt: You add a word to your sentence. What should you do next?
pool.hint: A change can make a new slip.
pool.explain: Read it again. A new word can land in the wrong place, like 'a cat cat'.

pool.prompt: The teacher asks: 'Can you tell me more about the cake?' What should you write?
choices: A detail, like 'a big chocolate cake'
The words 'Can you tell me more?'
pool.hint: Answer the question. Do not copy it.
pool.explain: Add a detail that answers it, like 'a big chocolate cake'. Do not copy the question into your writing.
